item.title: Modeling the CNOT gate in Germanium double quantum dots
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first detailed, fast‑time simulation of a CNOT gate built from exchange‑coupled hole spins in Ge/GeSi double quantum dots, showing how a compact dressed singlet–triplet basis can replace costly configuration‑interaction calculations. By pinpointing non‑adiabatic barrier ramps, AC Stark shifts and charge‑noise hotspots as the dominant fidelity killers, it gives concrete design targets for microwave driving and gate‑voltage control that are directly relevant to the emerging CMOS‑compatible spin‑qubit roadmap. The work therefore bridges theory and experiment, helping the community gauge how close germanium‑based platforms are to achieving the high‑fidelity two‑qubit operations needed for scalable quantum processors.

We model a controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate mediated by exchange interactions in a realistic Ge/GeSi hole spin-qubit device. We use for that purpose a computationally efficient framework based on a compact dressed basis of many-body singlet and triplet states, which enables fast time-dependent simulations that would be prohibitive within a conventional configuration-interaction approach. We discuss the dominant sources of infidelity in ideal (noise-free) devices. On the one hand, the nonadiabaticity of the tunnel barrier ramps, enhanced by the transverse component of the exchange interaction, imposes limits on the speed of the CNOT gate. On the other hand, the AC Stark shift of the conditional resonance and the off-resonant driving of the complementary transition can significantly degrade the gate fidelity and call for a careful optimization of the driving conditions. Finally, we investigate the impact of quasi-static charge noise on the fidelity of the CNOT gate. We find that the capture of charges near the qubits can strongly disrupt the conditional operation, while the nanometer-scale motion of charges results in a loss of fidelity that sensitively depends on the position and strength of the corresponding dipole. Our results quantify the requirements on barrier control, microwave driving, and charge-noise stability for high-fidelity two-qubit operations in Ge/GeSi hole-spin qubits.

item.title: Twist-controlled imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a rigorously controllable way to trigger the imaginary‑time Mpemba effect in spin lattices by applying spatially patterned “twist” rotations that selectively populate high‑energy modes while leaving entanglement structure untouched. By isolating spectral‑weight redistribution as the sole driver of accelerated relaxation, the work provides a concrete analytical toolkit for speeding up ground‑state preparation—a long‑standing bottleneck for variational quantum imaginary‑time evolution and related algorithms. The authors validate the mechanism on interacting XXZ chains and even on a twelve‑qubit circuit simulation, suggesting that near‑term devices could exploit these twists to reduce convergence times without additional hardware overhead. While promising, practical deployment will still need careful calibration of twist profiles and error mitigation to preserve the delicate mode selection in noisy quantum processors.

We construct a controllable imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems using spatially modulated local rotations without changing initial bipartite entanglement spectra and correlation magnitudes. This feature unambiguously isolates the redistribution of spectral weights as the sole driver of the anomalous relaxation. Using the compact-boson description, we reveal that these twists act as precise mode selectors: higher-harmonic twists exclusively populate high-energy standing waves, structurally bypassing slow-decaying infrared modes to accelerate convergence. We derive exact analytical crossing times for these reversals and demonstrate that intentionally reintroducing the slow-mode population systematically delays the ITME. This exact mechanism is validated beyond the fixed-point theory via calculations on interacting XXZ chains and ladders. Furthermore, a twelve-qubit simulation of variational quantum imaginary-time evolution reproduces the reversals and their controlled delay, providing a concrete route to realize this protocol in realistic quantum circuits. Ultimately, these results provide a strictly controllable and exact starting point for realizing and investigating the imaginary-time Mpemba effect, establishing a foundational paradigm to harness anomalous non-equilibrium relaxation in quantum ground-state preparations.

item.title: Bell-pair distillation under imperfect operations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the Bell‑pair distillation protocol introduced last year can still boost entanglement fidelity even when the underlying gates and measurements are noisy, a crucial step toward deploying entanglement purification on near‑term hardware. By mapping out which incoherent versus coherent error regimes preserve the advantage—and revealing how asymmetric errors can be balanced through complementary postselection—the work links theoretical guarantees to realistic quantum‑network nodes and sensing platforms. The findings suggest that modest‑quality devices could already benefit from built‑in entanglement cleaning, though the protocol’s tolerance varies sharply with error type, underscoring the need for tailored calibration in practical deployments.

We recently proposed an entanglement distillation protocol based on local operations and classical communication that probabilistically and universally distills a maximally entangled Bell pair from multiple copies of an unknown two-qubit state [Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 260202 (2025)]. Here, we investigate the robustness of this protocol against imperfections in its implementation. We consider several incoherent and coherent gate-error models, as well as measurement readout errors, and determine the regimes in which distillation enhances the fidelity with the target Bell state. We find that the protocol remains effective over substantial error ranges, although its robustness depends strongly on the type of error. We further analyze asymmetric errors between the two parties and identify conditions under which complementary postselection outcomes yield identical distillation dynamics, allowing the success probability to be enhanced.

item.title: Quantum computation of energy level degeneracy and thermodynamical properties of spin systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a practical route for extracting full energy‑level degeneracies and thermodynamic observables from noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices by measuring the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures with just a single ancilla qubit. By leveraging an exact inverse discrete Fourier transform on spectra that lie on an equally spaced grid, the authors avoid spectral leakage and achieve near‑exact reconstruction of degeneracies—even on a 36‑spin frustrated Kagome Ising model run on IBM’s Kingston processor—showcasing how clever circuit ordering can tame depth‑related noise. The result is a proof‑of‑principle that thermodynamic quantities such as heat capacity can be reliably estimated on current hardware, opening the door to quantum‑assisted studies of complex many‑body materials without requiring full phase‑estimation or large ancillary registers.

We propose a hybrid quantum-classical method for reconstructing energy-level degeneracies and thermodynamic properties of spin systems. A single ancilla qubit is used to measure the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures. For spectra lying on a known equally spaced energy grid, the inverse discrete Fourier transform allows exact reconstruction of degeneracies in the absence of noise, without spectral leakage. The quantum circuits are optimized using commuting interactions and Eulerian ordering. We demonstrate the method for frustrated Ising antiferromagnets on periodic Kagome graphs with up to 36 spins, using the ibm_kingston quantum processor. Despite substantial circuit depth and hardware noise, the reconstructed spectra retain their dominant features, and the calculated heat capacities reproduce the main temperature dependence of the exact results. Keywords: partition function, imaginary temperature, Ising model, heat capacity, ancilla qubit, quantum computing.

item.title: Electron-photon entanglement in real space from quantum electrodynamics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first fully real‑space, time‑resolved simulation of electron–photon entanglement generated by scattering in a nonrelativistic QED framework, going beyond the usual rotating‑wave approximation and single‑mode models. By showing how the transient global entanglement peaks during an off‑resonant pulse while local entropy patterns map the dipole coupling strength, it provides a concrete benchmark for emerging waveguide‑QED platforms that aim to harness strong light–matter interactions for hybrid quantum processors. The results also clarify where photons are created and absorbed in space, offering practical guidance for designing nanophotonic structures that minimize decoherence while maximizing controllable entanglement.

We study the entanglement between an electron and the photon it scatters, resolved in real space and time. Starting from nonrelativistic QED in Fermi's oscillator representation, we write Fock's coupled equations for components with fixed photon number in the photon configuration space, in the length gauge, where the photon is created around the atom through a nonlocal kernel. Truncated at one photon, the equations are solved numerically without the rotating-wave approximation for a one-dimensional model atom in a waveguide with a single transverse mode and enhanced coupling. The atom is driven by a short, off-resonant laser pulse, with the electron and photon represented on real-space grids. The global electron-photon entanglement is largely transient. It peaks during the pulse and decreases as the polarized electron cloud returns to the core, leaving a state close to a product of the electron state and a superposition of the field vacuum with a single scattered photon. Local entanglement, obtained from walkers sampled across both photon-number components, exhibits opposite spatial patterns for the two particles. The electron entropy is smallest at the nucleus and maps the local strength of the dipole coupling, whereas the photon entropy is largest near the atom, where photons are created and absorbed, and smaller in the outgoing wave packets.

item.title: Multimode continuous-variable quantum key distribution with CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic integration
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first CMOS‑compatible multimode continuous‑variable QKD system, showing that silicon‑photonic transmitters and receivers can jointly generate and detect two polarization channels with >20 dB shot‑noise clearance and a finite‑size secret‑key rate of 6.7 Mbit/s over deployed fiber. By integrating a dual‑channel transimpedance amplifier and using digital unitary recovery to eliminate active polarization control, the work bridges the gap between laboratory‑scale QKD demonstrations and mass‑manufacturable hardware, echoing recent pushes toward fully integrated quantum communication chips. The multimode security analysis also reveals that modest crosstalk (≈2 %) can nearly double the secure distance compared with single‑mode estimates, highlighting a practical pathway to high‑throughput, scalable quantum‑secured networks. Readers should note that while the results are compelling, extending beyond two modes and maintaining low crosstalk will be key challenges for future deployments.

Multiplexing and photonic-electronic integration offer a route to scalable and high-throughput quantum key distribution (QKD) networks through parallel transmission and compact hardware suited to volume manufacturing. Realizing this route requires multichannel transmitters and receivers, and a security analysis accounting for mode coupling. Here we present a CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic multimode continuous-variable QKD architecture, using polarization multiplexing as a two-mode example. Silicon-photonic transmitter and receiver chips prepare and detect two polarization modes in parallel. The receiver is co-integrated with a dual-channel 28-nm CMOS transimpedance amplifier, providing shot-noise clearances exceeding 20 dB in both channels. Pilot-assisted unitary digital recovery removes the need for active optical polarization control, while a multimode security analysis accounts for the mode crosstalk. At 2 percent residual crosstalk, the multimode analysis extends the simulated secure distance from 39 to 84 km, near the crosstalk-free limit of 89 km. Over 10 km of deployed fibre, the mean total finite-size secret-key rate estimate is 6.69 Mbit/s, 12 percent above the single-mode analysis from the same digitally recovered data. These results establish a route to scalable multimode quantum-secured networks built on technology suited to mass production.

item.title: Quantum-Classical Framework for the Joint Optimization of Bidirectional EV Charging and Trip Assignment
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a hybrid quantum‑classical Benders decomposition can tackle the notoriously hard joint scheduling of bidirectional EV charging and trip assignment, introducing logic‑based conflict cuts that sidestep the qubit overhead normally required for feasibility constraints. By sparsifying the state‑of‑charge formulation and demonstrating MILP‑optimal results on benchmark problems—and even running a tiny instance on IBM’s quantum processor—the work bridges recent advances in quantum optimization (e.g., QAOA and annealing) with real‑world energy‑mobility challenges. While still at proof‑of‑concept scale, the approach hints that future quantum accelerators could become practical tools for managing distributed energy assets in smart‑grid fleets.

The integration of bidirectional (V2G) charging allows electric vehicle (EV) fleets to operate as distributed energy assets. However, the joint optimization of charging schedules and trip assignments is NP-hard. Moreover, bidirectional power flows create non-monotonic state-of-charge (SoC) dynamics that weaken standard dual-based Benders cuts. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical Benders decomposition framework. To overcome the qubit overhead associated with encoding feasibility cuts, we introduce logic-based conflict cuts, which require near-zero auxiliary qubits. Furthermore, we develop a sparse recursive SoC formulation that reduces the constraint-matrix density by a factor of T/3 in the horizon length T. We demonstrate that our framework recovers MILP-optimal solutions on benchmark instances with a low auxiliary-qubit budget, and, as a minimal proof of concept, we execute a small instance end-to-end on IBM quantum hardware.

item.title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a critical bottleneck for large‑scale superconducting processors by showing that both two‑qubit and single‑qubit gates can be driven with frequency‑division multiplexed microwave pulses, cutting the number of control lines needed by up to two orders of magnitude. The demonstrated 1:4 parallel CZ and XY(π/2) gate fidelities—6.4 × 10⁻³ and 1.06 × 10⁻³ respectively—match conventional single‑line performance, indicating that multiplexing does not sacrifice error rates. By completing an all‑microwave control stack, the work paves the way for denser qubit layouts within the limited cooling power of dilution refrigerators, a prerequisite for the millions of physical qubits required by fault‑tolerant architectures. The results still rely on careful band‑pass filtering and may need further scaling studies, but they provide a concrete path toward hardware‑efficient quantum error correction.

Universal fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers are expected to require millions of physical qubits; yet extending the prevailing dedicated-control-line paradigm to this scale would exceed the wiring density and cooling-power budget of dilution refrigerators. Microwave frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) revolutionized classical communications by enabling many independent channels to share common transmission infrastructure. Translating this principle to superconducting quantum control, however, requires an all-microwave architecture and experimental validation of frequency-multiplexed gate control. Recent work in quantum error correction has demonstrated microwave-based readout, single-qubit gates and leakage suppression, whereas two-qubit gates remain predominantly driven by unipolar pulses and thus constitute the missing element of an all-microwave architecture. Here, we propose a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework in which all gate operations are frequency-division multiplexed using polychromatic microwave pulses and band-pass filters, thereby reducing the required control-line count by one to two orders of magnitude. In a 1:4 demonstration, we achieve average errors of $(6.4\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$ for parallel FDM CZ gates and $(10.6\pm0.2)\times10^{-4}$ for parallel FDM $XY(π/2)$ gates, without statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation. Together with on-chip DC sources, this FDM-based gate-control scheme completes the last missing module in a scalable multiplexed-control architecture toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Comparing classical and quantum QUBO solvers: optimality, trajectory diagnostics, and limits of solver selection
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it provides the most systematic head‑to‑head benchmark yet between classical exact solvers, tensor‑network methods and a fixed‑schedule quantum algorithm on realistic QUBO instances up to 128 variables, revealing that mature branch‑and‑cut techniques still outpace current quantum approaches for solution quality and optimality certification. By dissecting trajectory diagnostics such as bond dimension growth and identifying warm‑start trapping in DMRG sweeps, the authors show where tensor‑network methods have untapped potential but also why simple rules for solver selection remain elusive. The finding that a linear‑ramp QAOA offers no advantage over classical comparators underscores the need for more sophisticated quantum schedules or hybrid strategies before quantum hardware can claim practical superiority on combinatorial optimization problems.

Comparing solvers for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) requires distinguishing solution quality from optimality certification. We compare classical, tensor-network, and fixed-schedule quantum approaches on 180 benchmark instances from ten families with 14-48 variables, supplemented by harder synthetic instances with known optimal solutions, extending to 128 variables. On the main benchmark, a general-purpose branch-and-cut solver matches all reference energies and certifies 176 instances within a 600,s cap. When the known optima are moved to randomly chosen bitstrings, the search comparison changes: at n = 48 the branch-and-cut solver finds only four of ten optima and certifies none, whereas parallel tempering reaches every optimum in every tested run at a 60,s budget. Structural and trajectory diagnostics explain aspects of tensor-network performance. A treewidth bound ranks trajectory bond-dimension demand at Spearman $ρ= 0.78$ in sample and $0.73$ out of sample, but provides only a coarse runtime estimate. Controlled experiments identify excited-state trapping during warm-started density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) sweeps and demonstrate mitigation by restarting the variational search. These diagnostics do not yield a validated solver-selection rule. The tested linear-ramp quantum approximate optimization algorithm (LR-QAOA) runs offer no solution-quality improvement over the classical comparators. In the separate Wishart scaling study, on the harder setting, none of the classical methods tested reaches the optimum at the sampled sizes from n = 72 onward within the tested budgets. While this does not provide evidence for quantum advantage, it identifies a domain for further investigation.

item.title: Modulation and protection of entanglement in a two-qubit system via two interacting oscillator control
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how deliberately coupling auxiliary harmonic oscillators can actively shape the decoherence landscape of two qubits, offering a rare analytical treatment that links oscillator stability to entanglement dynamics. By demonstrating regimes where position‑position and momentum‑momentum interactions revive or suppress concurrence—even in the presence of thermal dissipation—the work extends recent reservoir‑engineering approaches that use bosonic modes as protective “quantum buses.” If experimentally realized, such engineered oscillator networks could become a lightweight hardware layer for preserving entanglement on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum processors.

We investigate the control and protection of two-qubit entanglement through engineered interactions between two auxiliary harmonic oscillators. Each qubit is coupled to a local oscillator via a dephasing interaction, while the oscillators interact through independently tunable position-position and momentum-momentum couplings. Employing the characteristic-function representation, we obtain analytical solutions for the composite-system dynamics and examine how the stability properties of the coupled oscillators determine the evolution of two-qubit concurrence. Our analysis reveals distinct dynamical regimes exhibiting entanglement revivals, suppression, or decay, and identifies configurations in which oscillator interactions effectively reduce entanglement degradation. We further investigate the influence of thermal dissipation using local and global master-equation descriptions, demonstrating that suitable oscillator couplings can preserve substantial two-qubit entanglement under the dissipative conditions considered. These results establish a connection between the dynamical stability of auxiliary bosonic modes and the controllability of entanglement in discrete-variable quantum systems, providing a potential strategy for entanglement protection through engineered oscillator interactions.

item.title: Supercurrent enables the reading of quantum information without destroying it
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports a new technique that uses a supercurrent to perform a quantum‑non‑demolition readout of a qubit, allowing the state to be inferred without causing collapse. By leveraging dissipation‑free superconducting currents, the method sidesteps the trade‑off between measurement fidelity and back‑action that has limited many superconducting processors, complementing recent progress in dispersive readout and error‑corrected logical qubits. If scalable, such nondestructive sensing could simplify syndrome extraction in surface‑code architectures and reduce overhead for quantum error correction, though integration with existing control hardware remains an open challenge.

One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it.

item.title: Maximal Orbital Entanglement from Non-Interacting Fermions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that even the simplest mean‑field states—Slater determinants of non‑interacting fermions—can saturate the theoretical limit of orbital entanglement for a wide range of particle numbers and lattice sizes, overturning the common belief that free‑fermion wavefunctions are useless as quantum resources. Orbital rotations are used in quantum many-body physics and chemistry to reduce the complexity of quantum states by compressing their correlation into a small set of relevant orbitals. In striking contrast, quantum information processing strives for the opposite: orbitals that maximize entanglement as a resource. Motivated by this, we prove that Slater determinants of $N$ fermions on a lattice of $d_A + d_B = d$ sites, although free of particle correlation, can carry up to $\min\{d_A, d_B, N, d-N\}$ ebits of orbital entanglement. Given enough particles and holes, this equals the maximum over all fermionic states. For arbitrary free states, we derive the maximal orbital total correlation in closed form for all bipartitions, the finest partition, and all partitions of up to five sites, using new majorization relations for Hermitian matrices. Taken together, these results turn mean-field states, the starting point of most many-body methods in physics and chemistry, into a viable resource for quantum information processing.

item.title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a distributed quantum‑centric supercomputing framework can break large electronic‑structure problems into smaller fragments that fit on near‑term quantum processors, dramatically cutting qubit counts, circuit depth and sampling cost while still capturing inter‑fragment correlations through a clever two‑step aggregation scheme. By pairing the physics‑informed generative SQD solver with an additional generative model to identify the most important sectors of Hilbert space, the authors achieve up to a 95 % reduction in diagonalization size for water and formamide dimers—an advance that dovetails with recent fragment‑based VQE and quantum embedding efforts. If the approach scales to bigger molecules, it could make high‑accuracy quantum chemistry simulations feasible on today’s hybrid HPC‑quantum platforms, though the overall workflow still relies on substantial classical post‑processing and careful error mitigation.

Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.

item.title: Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how resonant inelastic X‑ray scattering can be turned from a passive probe into an active source of heralded entanglement between distant regions of a solid, essentially bringing the DLCZ quantum‑network recipe into the hard‑X‑ray regime. By demonstrating that pathway‑entangled photons can project a material onto maximally entangled edge excitations—whether simple two‑site Bell pairs or fractionalized spins in an AKLT chain—the work opens a new route for linking quantum‑matter platforms to photonic quantum information processing. The proposal is timely because it leverages emerging X‑ray interferometry and ultrafast detectors, but its practical impact will hinge on achieving sufficient phase stability and photon‑count rates in realistic scattering experiments.

Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.

item.title: One-sided-DIQKD using any pure bipartite entangled state secure against all attacks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that one‑sided‑device‑independent QKD can be made secure with any pure bipartite entangled state, eliminating the need for costly maximally‑entangled resources and expanding the usable regime to nearly separable states. By linking security directly to quantum steering rather than full Bell nonlocality, it aligns with recent efforts to relax device‑trust assumptions while still protecting against all attacks, a step forward from earlier qubit‑only, fully‑device‑independent schemes. The practical upshot is that existing telecom‑grade sources and detectors could already support robust key generation in realistic networks, though the required detection efficiencies and visibilities must still meet the thresholds identified for each state.

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) allows spatially separated parties to establish a secret key among themselves based on quantum principles. While QKD systems are being deployed worldwide, their reliance on trusted measurements makes them vulnerable. Moreover, existing protocols have largely focussed on the qubit cases, and rely on the maximally entangled state, a costly resource to generate. Here, we consider the one-sided-device-independent (1SDI) QKD protocols, where one of the measurement devices is trusted while the other is untrusted. The resource in this scenario is quantum steering, an asymmetric form of quantum nonlocality. This is inspired by a real-world scenario, where the trusted party can be considered to be a bank, or any large organisation that has sufficient resources to protect its systems and validate them, while the users are vulnerable to attacks. We then demonstrate that a secure key can be obtained using any pure bipartite entangled state in this setup. Considering realistic detectors and sources based on current technology, we demonstrate that even states that are almost separable can be used to extract a secure key. Moreover, for every pure entangled bipartite state, we find the critical detection efficiencies and visibility to obtain a secure key.

item.title: Fermion Scattering on Quantum Computers
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks one of the first concrete demonstrations that a hybrid qubit‑qumode processor can simulate real‑time fermion–antifermion scattering and resolve resonance formation in a (1+1)‑dimensional Yukawa model, providing a practical benchmark for near‑term quantum hardware. By combining digital encoding of fermions with continuous‑variable representation of the scalar field, the authors bridge the gap between abstract quantum‑field‑theory algorithms and experimentally accessible photonic platforms, complementing recent tensor‑network studies of low‑dimensional QFT dynamics. The ability to extract decay rates and Breit–Wigner resonance profiles with percent‑level accuracy shows that local observables on hybrid devices can already probe nontrivial particle physics phenomena, though scaling to higher dimensions and larger lattices will still demand significant advances in error mitigation and hardware connectivity.

Resonant scattering links particle interactions to the formation and decay of unstable excitations. We develop a hybrid quantum-computing framework to study these dynamics through fermion--antifermion collisions. Our formulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional Yukawa theory encodes fermions in qubits and the scalar field in qumodes. We identify the operations needed for a photonic implementation and benchmark the dynamics with tensor-network simulations. Near resonance, we resolve the build-up of a localised scalar excitation and the subsequent partial return of energy to the fermions. Enhanced entanglement accompanies this exchange. Time-dependent correlator measurements reproduce the analytically predicted decay rate to a few percent precision, with energy scans exhibiting a resonance peak consistent with packet-averaged Breit--Wigner behaviour. These results establish a concrete scattering benchmark for hybrid quantum computers and demonstrate how local real-time observables can probe particle-resonance dynamics.

item.title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces HERMES, a method that shifts the entire linear‑combination‑of‑unitaries (LCU) processing from quantum hardware to classical post‑processing, eliminating ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and the explosion of circuit repetitions that have limited LCU techniques on NISQ and early fault‑tolerant devices. By expanding both the operator and observable in the Pauli basis and using a two‑level measurement‑reduction scheme, HERMES keeps the number of distinct measurement settings fixed while still delivering accurate expectation values, a practical advance over recent randomized LCU approaches that scale linearly with sample count. The demonstrated performance on H₂ and LiH ground‑state energy estimation shows that shallow, gate‑light circuits can now be leveraged for variational simulations without the heavy hardware overhead previously assumed necessary. If the classical sampling overhead remains manageable, this could broaden the applicability of LCU‑based algorithms across chemistry, sensing and beyond.

Estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$ for a quantum state evolved under a general, possibly non-unitary, operator $A$ is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms. Existing linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) approaches implement $A$ on hardware, requiring ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and, in randomized variants, fresh circuit executions for every Monte Carlo sample. These costs are prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices. We propose HERMES (Hardware-Efficient Reusable Measurements for Estimating LCU-based expectation valueS), which moves the processing of $A$ entirely to the classical domain. Expanding $A$ and $O$ in the Pauli basis and sampling pairs of Pauli terms classically, HERMES rewrites $μ= \mathrm{Tr}(OAρA^{\dagger})/\mathrm{Tr}(AρA^{\dagger})$ as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state $ρ$, with no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of $A$. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of the sample count, unlike randomized LCU methods whose circuit executions grow linearly with it. On ground-state energy estimation of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{LiH}$ via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is also more robust to noise and completes a noisy $\mathrm{LiH}$ simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead growing with the number of Pauli terms in $A$.

item.title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it translates the abstract promise of quantum machine learning into concrete language that radiologists can actually grasp, highlighting how NISQ‑era hardware could one day alleviate the massive compute demands of modern deep‑learning pipelines. By cataloguing existing hybrid quantum‑classical approaches—such as variational circuits and quantum image encodings—and showing early results on tasks like tumor classification, it situates quantum methods within the broader push toward more efficient medical imaging analytics while making clear that current demonstrations are limited to tiny datasets and simulators. Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.

The duration decreases rapidly with increasing relative outer-qubit coupling and becomes weakly dependent on the middle-qubit coupling in the stronger-coupling regime. item.title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a broad class of quantum‑machine‑learning models can be pre‑trained entirely on classical hardware by propagating observables backward through the circuit with Pauli propagation, sidestepping the costly parameter‑shift gradients that have limited scalability so far. By introducing weight‑ and degree‑based truncations plus pruning heuristics, the authors make the method tractable for 64‑qubit shallow ansätze and demonstrate successful deployment on IBM’s ibm_berlin processor for both a VQE Ising study and a binary‑image generative model. The result is a practical pathway to train larger quantum models with far fewer parametrized gates than IQP‑style circuits, reducing transpilation overhead and bringing near‑term quantum advantage within reach—though the approach currently relies on shallow depth and approximation choices that must be validated for deeper architectures.

Scaling parametrized quantum circuits to a larger number of qubits is a central challenge in Quantum Machine Learning: gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule quickly becomes prohibitively expensive, while gradient-free optimizers offer limited convergence guarantees. We apply the Pauli propagation framework to a broad class of Quantum Machine Learning problems in which the loss is expressed as a function of expectation values of the circuit's observables, while keeping the relevant quantity of interest, such as the quantum state or its samples, classically intractable to compute. By propagating the observables backward through the circuit, we obtain an explicit parametric expression for the loss that can be minimized entirely on classical hardware. We also present complementary strategies to make propagation tractable at large scale, including weight-based and degree-based truncations and pruning heuristics. We demonstrate the approach on two benchmarks run on 64-qubit circuits: Variational Quantum Eigensolver on a two-dimensional Ising model, and training of a discrete-type generative model for binary images. In both cases, the classically pre-trained parameters are deployed on the IBM quantum processor ibm_berlin. For generative learning, we additionally show that the circuits considered here require substantially fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style ansätze, reducing transpilation overhead and making deployment on current quantum hardware feasible.

item.title: LYNX - A trapped-ion quantum information processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases LYNX, a trapped‑ion processor that pushes ion‑based hardware into the same performance tier as leading superconducting systems by delivering sub‑10⁻⁴ single‑qubit errors and two‑qubit errors below 3×10⁻³ across a 24‑qubit register. The all‑to‑all connectivity and a demonstrated quantum volume of 2¹⁵ signal that trapped ions can now support deep, highly entangled circuits at scales relevant for early error‑corrected algorithms. While the QV benchmark stops at 15 qubits, the reported gate fidelities suggest LYNX is poised to accelerate both quantum‑chemistry simulations and the development of fault‑tolerant logical qubits on ion platforms.

We introduce LYNX, a quantum information processor based on trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions. It utilizes up to 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity. We characterize the system performance using rigorous benchmarks, such as randomized benchmarking (RB), GHZ state fidelity estimates, and quantum volume (QV) tests. The LYNX processor shows average 1-qubit gate errors of $8(5)\times 10^{-5}$ tested via standard RB in a 24-qubit register. An average 2-qubit gate error in a 24-qubit register of $2.84(8)\times 10^{-3}$ is demonstrated using interleaved RB. Furthermore, the device passes QV tests using up to 15 qubits which corresponds to a quantum volume of QV$=2^{15}$.

item.title: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a concrete step toward fault‑tolerant quantum computing by showing that logical qubits encoded in surface codes can be created, entangled and teleported on a real superconducting processor with error rates below the 1 % threshold for each round of error correction. By combining component selection, fast reset to suppress leakage, and noise‑aware decoding, the IBM Phoenix team pushes distance‑5 surface‑code performance into a regime where logical operations begin to outpace raw physical errors—a milestone that aligns with recent advances in lattice‑surgery protocols and multi‑round stabilizer cycles reported by other groups. The demonstrated logical Bell fidelities above 93 % and teleportation of gates suggest that near‑term applications such as error‑corrected quantum sensing or small‑scale algorithmic primitives could soon be run on hardware that already incorporates the essential ingredients for scalable fault tolerance.

We demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations using \texttt{ibm\_phoenix}, a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits that are capable of fast reset. Using strategies to exclude underperforming components together with noise informed decoding, we routinely produce surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with logical error per round below 1\%. We demonstrate entanglement between two logical qubits, where logical Bell-state fidelities above 93\% are observed for entanglement created via lattice surgery. With three logical qubits and lattice surgery, we perform logical teleportation of a range of states and gates, observing fidelities in the range 78\% - 93\%. Using reset to reduce qubit leakage, we show that repeated rounds of stabilizer measurements continue to exhibit improvements in a stability experiment up to $\sim 2\cdot 10^{-7}$ over 170 measurement rounds.

item.title: Finite Nonsignalling Resources Suffice to Simulate Entangled Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a decades‑old open problem by proving that any pure two‑qubit entangled state can be reproduced exactly with only a finite number of PR‑boxes and shared randomness, eliminating the need for continuous‑alphabet resources or communication. By giving an explicit worst‑case bound that scales modestly with the Schmidt angle, it clarifies the resource hierarchy in Bell nonlocality and shows that the apparent continuity of quantum correlations does not demand infinite‑dimensional simulators. While the construction is presently a theoretical tool rather than a hardware blueprint, it opens new avenues for efficient classical‑plus‑non‑signalling simulations of entangled systems and deepens our understanding of what underlies quantum advantage in sensing and communication protocols.

A longstanding question in Bell nonlocality is whether finite-alphabet nonsignalling resources can reproduce the continuum of measurement correlations of partially entangled qubits. Here we resolve this problem by showing that every fixed pure two-qubit state admits an exact simulation of all local projective-measurement statistics using shared randomness and finitely many Popescu-Rohrlich (PR) boxes, without communication or postselection. The boxes operate in parallel, with a worst-case bound independent of the measurement settings: at most $128\cot^4θ$ calls for the Schmidt state $\cosθ|00\rangle+\sinθ|11\rangle$, $0<θ<π/4$. The key is an exact finite-selection method that reduces input-dependent continuous sampling to a choice from a fixed-length shared random list, implemented through a finite PR-box network. The construction extends to arbitrary mixed two-qubit states and local binary-outcome POVMs. This reveals a fundamental separation between the continuity of quantum measurement correlations and the alphabet size of the resources needed to simulate them, shedding light on the resource-theoretic structure of Bell nonlocality.
